newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - London's money market turns back on bygone era.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - London's money market turns back on bygone era.

text.p: One of the more colourful aspects of London's money markets -- an antiquated system for trading short-term debts -- comes to an end on Monday after more than a century of tradition.
But the men at the heart of this trade, known as the discount bill market, say they are now ready to move forward.

A series of reforms by the Bank of England, announced last year, mark the end of a system steeped in history. Just 15 years ago top-hatted gentlemen bought and sold money market bills in person in one of the world's most advanced financial centres.
But the prospect of a single European currency and the pace of technological change have forced the reforms as London battles to remain the hub of international finance.

"These are the most radical reforms for discount houses this century," said Christopher Chapman, chairman of Seccombe, Marshall and Campion, which has been a discount house since 1922 and was agent to the Bank of England for some 60 years.
"But we welcome the changes as they confirm our view that we had to change to adapt to a highly competitive world."
FROM 1800 TO THE 21ST CENTURY

The Bank of England's reforms strip the discount houses of their exclusive right to rediscount eligible bills with the central bank. They widen the range of participants in the Bank's money market dealings and introduce so-called gilt repos in daily money market operations.
But the former discount houses, some of which can trace their lineage back to the early 1800s, are confident they can ride the wave of change and even strengthen their positions.
"There are very good reasons to assume our position will actually be stronger," said Ian Perkins, director of the Gerrard Group and chairman of discount house Gerrard and King.
"People assume that because the Bank has in effect removed our licences, they have removed our business. But they haven't at all."
London's discount house system was primarily a street market, with pinstripe-suited men mulling over the direction of the market in the cramped back streets of London's financial district.

The hallmark of the broker was his silk tophat, and right up to the early 1980s he would walk into one bank, buy a bill of exchange, cross the road and sell it to another bank. This practice continued long after sophisticated computer dealing systems made electronic trading the norm.
Chapman of Seccombe's said he still has three silk hats, the first of which he bought in 1967 for 18 pounds ($29.1).
COMPETITIVE PRESSURES
But competition from other cities and the move towards European monetary union have forced London to change.
Gerrard and King's Perkins said the new system would improve market liquidity.
In the past, these firms held exclusive rights to rediscount short-term bills -- effectively IOUs issued by companies and guaranteed by banks-- with the Bank.

One of Monday's reforms strips discount houses of that lucrative right and opens up this trade to a range of other firms. The Bank took this step because the discount houses could not cope with its daily market needs.
"As the only people able to deal with the Bank in eligible bills...the total pile of bills was probably not big enough to deal with the daily shortages," Perkins said.
As a result, prices of these bills at times were forced up to unrealistic levels.

Britain's discount bill system is the last of several such markets that once flourished in the Commonwealth, a group of countries which each owe allegiance to the British monarch. A few of these markets remain in less developed countries.
"They're trying to engender a discount market in Nigeria...but out of mature money markets Britain's is probably the one that remained the longest," Chapman said.

Another major reform is the inclusion in daily money market trade of "repurchase agrements" -- or repos -- for British government bonds. These are agreements where one party loans a security to another for a specified period of time. As a result, the market can become much more liquid.
"If the repo is going to augment liquidity, it should have the effect of smoothing out an imbalance at the very short end of the money market," Perkins said.
VICTIMS AND VICTORS

One discount house to fall casualty to the Bank's changes is Union Plc. Once a pillar of the London financial scene, Union said last Tuesday it would no longer be a money market counterparty to the Bank of England.
But money market veterans said Union was the exception rather than the rule, and they added it was highly unlikely the other five remaining discount houses would follow suit.
One way the discount houses are preparing to do battle in the new, tougher money market, is by merging their activities with parent companies.

Michael Walker, chairman of discount house Clive Securities Group, said his firm was merging its securities activities with the private banking arm of its parent company, South Africa's Investec Bank Ltd.
And Chapman said Seccombe Marshall and Campion was to become the London branch of its parent company, Compagnie Parisienne de Reescompte.
Monday's reforms have been well flagged and most discount houses have diversified their business in anticipation.
"We have been trying to get away from being just a discount house to being a more broadly based financial institution," said Walker.

He said around only 10-15 percent of business was directly linked to their function as discount house. "The remaining include repo money markets, proprietary trading, bond lending and equity stock lending," he said.
Seccombe's Chapman said the reforms ensured Britain's compatability with its European neighbours.
"If EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union) comes about and we're part of it, our operations will be very much a part of the European way of doing things," he said.
This new way of doing things, of course, does not include silk hats, blue blood and old school ties.
($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
